story.headline: The Amazon's dry-season clearing front
story.what: New clearings (fishbone pattern) and fire along the BR-163 highway.
story.physics: Clear-cutting removes canopy volume: HV drops. Cloud and smoke never stop the radar, which is why SAR underpins near-real-time deforestation alerts.
story.drivers: Cattle pasture expansion, land grabbing along roads, soy logistics corridor.
story.caveats: Selective logging leaves canopy gaps below the 20 m pixel; HV change can be subtle.

story.headline: Monsoon floodwater along the Brahmaputra, seen through the cloud
story.what: Open floodwater spreading over farmland and villages along the Brahmaputra, then draining away.
story.physics: Calm water mirrors the radar pulse away from the satellite, so HH backscatter collapses (black). Where water sits beneath crops or trees, L-band's 24 cm wave bounces water->stem->satellite and HH turns brighter: the flooded-vegetation class optical satellites and C-band radar mostly miss.
story.drivers: Monsoon rain several times above normal in upper Assam, sediment-choked braided channels, embankment breaches, wetland loss and upstream deforestation.
story.caveats: Wind-roughened water can look bright; very smooth sand bars can look like water. Compare against GPM rainfall and gauge data.

story.headline: A summer of canopy loss in Huelva's plantations, seen through the smoke
story.what: 132 kmÂ² of HV canopy loss that begins between the 21 July and 14 August passes and keeps deepening into October - the pattern of a large summer fire followed by salvage clearing. Confirm the perimeter against EFFIS before calling all of it burn.
story.physics: Same HV volume-loss signature as forest fires elsewhere; Mediterranean eucalyptus/pine plantations give a strong pre-fire HV baseline.
story.drivers: Heatwaves, drought, plantation fuels, rural depopulation.
story.caveats: Harvest of plantation stands also lowers HV - confirm with EFFIS/FIRMS fire detections.

story.headline: Farming below sea level: Kuttanad's monsoon waters, through the cloud
story.what: Polder fields and backwater margins flood between the 6 and 18 August passes, stay inundated through September, peak on 5 October (574 kmÂ² of open water plus 251 kmÂ² of water under canopy) and have largely drained by 17 October.
story.physics: Open water is a mirror to the radar, so HH drops to near-black; water under rice or coconut canopy bounces water->stem->satellite and brightens HH. The HH/HV ratio separates the two.
story.drivers: Monsoon rain on a polder landscape that lies partly below sea level, river inflow from the Western Ghats, bund breaches and the Thanneermukkom barrage regime.
story.caveats: Polders are flooded on purpose for cultivation, so not all water is a disaster; separate managed flooding from inundation with dates and field context.

stats.note: largest on any date: 573.7 km² (05 Oct)

story.headline: A megacity sinking up to a few centimetres a month
story.what: Ground subsidence from aquifer over-pumping, accumulated over successive 12-day interferograms.
story.physics: Each 12-day pair measures line-of-sight shortening/lengthening; chaining pairs builds a displacement time series. Lake-bed clays compact as pore pressure drops.
story.drivers: Groundwater extraction for ~22 million people, compressible lacustrine clays of former Lake Texcoco.
story.caveats: Simple pair chaining accumulates noise; for publication-grade rates use SBAS (MintPy) on the full stack. Atmospheric delay in the rainy season adds cm-scale patterns.

story.headline: Watching a rice season breathe, field by field
story.what: Paddies are flooded for transplanting (dark), the canopy grows (bright), then harvest and residue burning reset them. Only fields showing the full flood-then-growth signature are labelled rice; fields with a weaker swing fall under 'other active cropland', so the rice figure is a lower bound.
story.physics: Flooded paddy = specular water, very dark. As rice tillers grow, volume scattering raises HV by 5-10 dB within weeks. The V-shaped HV curve is the radar fingerprint of rice. S-band responds more to leaves, L-band to stems and the soil-water interface.
story.drivers: Monsoon-timed transplanting, groundwater irrigation, procurement-driven rice monoculture, Aug-Sep 2026 floods that destroyed standing crops.
story.caveats: Rain on bare soil also brightens HH; use HV and the temporal shape, not single dates.

story.headline: An Oregon fire complex: canopy loss through the smoke
story.what: 141 kmÂ² of canopy loss accumulating from mid-July into October across grass, shrub and juniper country. The modest HV drop (about -2.4 dB) is what L-band sees when fuels with little canopy volume burn; forest fires drop further.
story.physics: HV (cross-pol) comes from multiple scattering inside the canopy. Burning removes that volume, so HV drops 3-6 dB and stays low; HH may briefly rise from exposed, rough, wet soil.
story.drivers: Low snowpack, drought, dry lightning, decades of fuel build-up.
story.caveats: Grass/shrub fires (e.g. Big Grass Fire) barely change L-band HV: there is little volume to lose. That is a physics result, not a failure.

story.headline: One of the world's fastest glaciers, tracked every 12 days
story.what: Ice surface speed from pixel offset tracking between repeat passes: the fast trunk runs at roughly 17-28 m/day through the season, the surrounding ice at 2-4 m/day.
story.physics: Phase interferometry fails on fast-flowing, melting ice (coherence is lost), so features are cross-correlated between images; L-band penetrates the snow surface and keeps texture through melt season.
story.drivers: Warm Atlantic water melting the floating tongue, summer melt lubricating the bed, seasonal ice-melange buttressing.
story.caveats: Offsets over 12 days near the calving front can exceed the search window; check the SNR layer. A single pair can under-read speed when surface melt destroys the texture being tracked - treat an isolated dip as tracking loss, not a slowdown.

stats.label: Trunk speed range
stats.note: 12-day pairs; an isolated dip is usually tracking loss in melt, not a slowdown

story.headline: Africa's largest wetland swells with the rains
story.what: Seasonal expansion of open water and flooded papyrus swamp along the White Nile.
story.physics: Flooded papyrus and grass produce strong HH double bounce at L-band - the swamp brightens as it floods, while open lagoons go dark.
story.drivers: East African rains feeding Lake Victoria and the White Nile, record lake levels since 2019-2020.
story.caveats: Floating vegetation mats move; very dense papyrus can saturate the signal.

story.headline: Two great earthquakes 39 seconds apart, measured to the centimetre
story.what: Co-seismic ground displacement from strike-slip rupture along the Caribbean-South American plate boundary.
story.physics: Interferometry compares the phase of two passes 12 days apart; each colour cycle of fringes is 11.9 cm of motion along the radar line of sight. L-band keeps coherence over the forested Cordillera de la Costa where C-band decorrelates.
story.drivers: Right-lateral shear between the Caribbean and South American plates (San Sebastian - El Pilar fault system).
story.caveats: LOS is 1-D: strike-slip motion is mostly horizontal, so ascending and descending tracks show different patterns; combine them for east/up. L-band ionosphere near the equator can add cm-scale ramps - the GUNW ionospheric screen is subtracted.

legend.note: one colour cycle = λ/2 of line-of-sight motion
